messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj was a 42-year-old South Asian man who worked as a tax inspector and had been married for over two decades. His life took an unexpected turn when he accidentally caused a serious injury to another person during a routine traffic stop. The event left him with vivid crash imagery, where scenes of cars hitting each other replayed relentlessly in his mind. He also found himself unable to attend funerals or visit cemeteries without feeling overwhelmed by grief and guilt. Raj had come to believe that he deserved the suffering he was enduring because of what happened, and this belief drove him to suppress thoughts about the trauma whenever possible. The thought, "I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened," often crept into his mind as a form of self-punishment. He also reminded himself that it could have been worse, but this downshifting did little to ease his burden. When Raj recalled the event, he sometimes heard snippets of conversations and sirens in his head, which added to his distress. His memory of the incident was fragmented; some moments were extremely clear while others remained a complete blank. This partial clarity and incomplete picture made him feel like he was only remembering parts of what happened, leaving a sense of incompleteness that haunted him. Raj's negative appraisals compounded his struggles. He felt permanently humiliated by what had occurred, believing that his beliefs about how the world works were completely destroyed. The idea that he should have protected others but failed gnawed at him relentlessly. These feelings of humiliation and shattered beliefs reinforced each other in a vicious cycle, making it difficult for Raj to move forward. The triggers he experienced, such as crash imagery and funerals, often led to his maladaptive strategies of punishing himself and suppressing thoughts about the trauma. The more vividly he remembered parts of the event, the stronger these negative appraisals became. His fragmented memories triggered powerful feelings of humiliation and a sense that he had failed those around him. Over time, Raj's work as a tax inspector became increasingly difficult. He avoided areas with traffic congestion or any situation where there was potential for an accident to occur again. This avoidance affected his ability to conduct thorough inspections and made it challenging to focus on the job at hand. His marriage also began to suffer; he withdrew from family activities, leading to tension and misunderstandings between him and his wife. Raj finally sought help when he realized that his guilt and self-blame were overwhelming both his professional life and personal relationships. He was most afraid of never being able to forgive himself for the accident and feared continuing to live with this profound sense of failure. On the other hand, he hoped that therapy could provide him with a way to process what happened and find some form of peace. In summary, Raj's experience of PTSD was characterized by powerful triggers, maladaptive coping strategies, fragmented memories, and pervasive negative appraisals. His triggers led to self-punishment and thought suppression, while his memory issues reinforced his feelings of humiliation and shattered beliefs. The cycle tightened over time, making it difficult for him to function effectively in both his personal and professional life. His journey to seek help was driven by a deep desire to find a way out of the suffocating grip of guilt and self-blame that had taken hold since the traumatic event.
